title: Investigatio motuum, quibus laminae et virgae elasticae contremiscunt

deep.reconstruction:
The page continues Euler's solution of the frequency equation for a transversely vibrating elastic rod. The equation is cos ω = 2/(e^ω + e^{-ω}), i.e. cos ω · cosh ω = 1. This is the characteristic equation of the free–free beam, and equally of the clamped–clamped beam. Here ω = βa, the rod length times the spatial wavenumber.

§17–17 (end): Euler writes ω = 3ϱ + Φ with ϱ = π/2 and n = e^{3ϱ} ≈ 111.31. Then cos ω = sin Φ ≈ Φ, and e^{±Φ} ≈ 1 ± Φ. The equation becomes Φ = 2n/(n²(1+Φ) + 1 − Φ) ≈ 2n/(n²+1) ≈ 2/n ≈ 1/56 rad, roughly one degree. So the first nonzero root is ω₁ ≈ 3π/2 + 1°.

§18: The next root lies in the 'fifth quadrant', a few arcminutes below 5π/2. The sixth and seventh quadrants, where cos < 0, contain no root. In the eighth quadrant there is a root imperceptibly above 7π/2. Later roots approach 9π/2, 11π/2, … ever more closely, alternating sides of the odd multiples of π/2.

§19: Neglecting the small corrections, ω_k ≈ (2k+1)π/2. The frequencies ∝ ω² c√(2gb)/(2a²) therefore go as 9 : 25 : 49 : 81 …. The first two partials stand in the ratio 25:9 ≈ 2.78, an octave plus a tritone (G → c♯). Euler concludes the rod's partials are mutually inharmonic, giving a 'very unpleasant dissonance' when sounded together.

The next page superposes all modes into the general solution, with arbitrary amplitudes C and phases ζ, and discusses the nodes of the fundamental. This is the standard modal analysis of the free–free Euler–Bernoulli beam.
errors: Euler's estimate Φ ≈ 2/n = 1/56 ≈ 0.0179 rad drops Φ in the denominator. The true correction is 4.73004 − 4.71239 ≈ 0.01765 rad (≈1.01°), an overestimate of about 2% but qualitatively right.
The stated deviations check out. 5π/2 − 7.85320 ≈ 0.00078 rad ≈ 2.7′ ('aliquot minuta prima'). 10.99561 − 7π/2 ≈ 0.00004 rad ≈ 8″ ('excessus sentiri nequeat').
The frequency ratio 25:9 uses the approximate roots. With the exact roots the ratio is (7.8532/4.7300)² ≈ 2.757. This is still an octave plus roughly a tritone, so the musical conclusion stands.
The argument on the previous page truncates the series cos ω·cosh ω = 1 − ω⁴/6 + ω⁸/2520 − …. Euler's claim that there is no root in the first quadrant is true but only heuristically justified there.

ideas.what: Asymptotic location of the roots of cos ω cosh ω = 1 near odd multiples of π/2, with first-order correction Φ ≈ 2e^{-ω}·(sign), alternating sides
ideas.modern_name: Asymptotics of free–free beam eigenvalues, β_k a ≈ (2k+1)π/2
ideas.usually_credited_to: Euler and Daniel Bernoulli (1740s); standard in Rayleigh's Theory of Sound (1877)
ideas.where_published: Euler, Methodus inveniendi (1744), Additamentum I (elastic curves/vibrations); E526 itself

ideas.what: Frequencies proportional to ω², giving inharmonic partial series 9:25:49:81 and the musical judgement octave + tritone
ideas.modern_name: Inharmonic overtone spectrum of a free bar (xylophone/tuning-fork physics)
ideas.where_published: Methodus inveniendi 1744 Add. I; E526 (1782); discussed by Truesdell 1960

deep.surprise_reason: This is the standard, well-documented treatment of free–free beam frequencies, already analysed by Truesdell. The numerical estimates are correct and nothing on the page is new to the literature.
transcription_corrections: The transcription is essentially faithful. In the image the lines 'sumi igitur circiter poterit Φ = 2/n = 1/56; vnde patet an-' and 'siue Φ = 2n/(nn+1) proxime' are typeset interleaved, but the reading order given is correct.
